newsitem.title: USA: Dow dogs and recent laggards perk up.
newsitem.headline: Dow dogs and recent laggards perk up.

text.p: Dogs and recent underachievers in the Dow industrials have started to perk up as investors seek out laggards in the bull market's record run, which some technicians say may point to trouble ahead.
Woolworth Corp broke out technically, up 1-1/4 to 24, while Westinghouse Electric Corp, up one to 21, was set to break out amid market talk of its spin-off plans.
But most surprising was Bethlehem Steel Corp, 1996's worst performing component and the only Dow stock trading lower than it was 15 years ago, was up 5/8 to 8-7/8.

"This is late in trend activity. It looks like blue chips can easily go higher but I tell my brokers 'Make sure you tell your client they're coming in late -- these things have had a good move.' I suggest the client have actual, or mental, stop-loss orders," said Ralph Bloch, chief technical analyst at Raymond James & Associates.

He said the buying of recent underachievers was spurred partly by the client's edict "buy me something that hasn't moved." But Bloch added, "If they're getting down to everything, even Bethlehem Steel -- God, spare us!"

Gregory Nie of EVEREN Securities said, "We've reached the point where the majority of stocks have participated (in the run). Once the laggards are in motion, where do we go for an encore? That becomes a more critical question. In a week or two, that question will surface."

Woolworth has been the Dow's most stellar performer in 1996 after rebounding from a dismal 1995. "It broke out today. February 1994 was the last time the stock traded this high. This sets the stage for a reaction move to the low-30s," said Ralph Acampora, director of technical research at Prudential Securities.

"Westinghouse was a dog but now there's the restructuring that has the stock close to breaking out. If it makes a new high of 22, it would be a clear breakout and the highest since October-November 1991. At least, the target would be the low- to mid-30s," he said.

As for Bethlehem Steel, technicians were intrigued by its move higher from its virtual deadlock near eight for the past month and a half. "Bethlehem Steel has been stepped on. It's been in a slow fade for a few years and will hopefully stay here (in the) 7-10 (range). It's the least attractive of the Dow stocks," Acampora said.
When told Bethlehem Steel was trading higher, William Raftery, technical analyst at Smith Barney, joked, "I thought I'd retire before I saw this."
But not all technicians agreed that a rebound in some laggards bode poorly for the market.

Acampora, one of the Street's biggest bulls, said the market remains "awesome," buoyed by "low inflation and low interest rates." Raftery declined to read into the strength in Westinghouse, Woolworth and Bethlehem. "Westinghouse is up for extraneous reasons and the general tone is people are moving into select economically sensitive issues."

Ken Tower, a technical analyst at UST Securities, said, "I would worry more when the current leadership (technology, oils and financials) falls off than focus on laggards starting to rise. There's almost at least a correction when there's a change in leadership."
"It's more important to look at the weakness in leaders than strength in the laggards," said Tower, who still finds "plenty of reasons to be bullish."

He noted 1996's best Dow performers were Woolworth, up 75 percent so far and then AlliedSignal Inc, up 49 percent. Tower said the worst performers for the year are Bethlehem Steel, down 40 percent, AT&T Corp, down 23 percent, and General Motors, up four percent.
